schema.id: stable within one run of the parser: <kind>-<page or work>-<n>
schema.type: word_wall | song | dialogue | name | shout | other
schema.source_page: UESP page title the text was read from
schema.revid: revision id of that page in the snapshot
schema.location_or_speaker: where the text stands or who speaks it, as the wiki gives it
schema.dovahzul: the dragon-language text, wiki spelling, newline = wiki line break; for dialogue: only the dragon-language segments of the line, one per line
schema.english: the translation or gloss that stands on the wiki, or null; never supplied by this parser
schema.notes: provenance of the gloss, wiki caveats, sic notes
schema.optional fields: subtype, shout, teaches_word_index, teaches_words, teaches_meanings, highlighted_dovahzul, highlighted_english, in_game, game, spelling, canon_status, translation_source, gloss_source, context (full line as shown on the wiki), segments (aligned dragon/gloss pairs), also_on (other snapshot pages with the same line), duplicate_of (id of an earlier record with the same dragon text), uncertain, needs_review, inscription_column, transliteration_column, rune_inscription, english_in_game, runes, how_stated, source_title

conventions: Word-wall and rune-table text keeps the wiki's rune-case: UPPER CASE = a one-letter rune, a lower-case pair (aa ah ei ey ii ir oo uu ur) = one two-letter rune.
Parentheses and square brackets inside english are the wiki's own: they mark words added for English grammar.

canon_status 'canon' means the dragon text is reported by the wiki from an official game, book or publication. It does not certify the English: see translation_source or gloss_source for where the English comes from.
Hover glosses on dialogue pages are written by wiki editors; they are not in-game text. Treat them as semi-canon readings.

Dialogue segments with gloss 'none on the wiki (word-list match)' were found by matching words against the wiki's own dictionary page and this corpus; that step is a heuristic and can miss or mis-cut a phrase. The 'context' field always holds the full line as the wiki prints it.
Name meanings are sentences written by wiki editors, mostly built from the dictionary; 'uncertain': true marks the wiki's own hedging (may, might, either, ...).
Records with duplicate_of repeat dragon text found on another page; they are kept for provenance and left out of the unique token count.

counts.token_rule: letters with inner apostrophes or hyphens count as one token; dialogue counts only its dragon-language segments

dialogue_word_list.note: headwords read (not modified) from Lore_Dragon_Language.wikitext when present, plus every word of the word walls, songs and shouts parsed here

discovery_on_2026-11-14.how: tools/ingest/fetch_corpus.py --discover: links out of and into Lore:Dragon_Language, 22 full-text searches over the content namespaces, 8 categories
discovery_on_2026-11-14.added_after_discovery: 2 (Lore:Vundeheim, Lore:Korvag Crag), found on the same day by a further search for "Word Wall's translation"; the fetch list now holds 330 titles
discovery_on_2026-11-14.not_fetched: About 1,040 titles: talk and user pages; ESO patch notes, item, pet and crown-store lists; Legends card lists; alphabetical Lore index pages (People, Places, Bestiary, Gods, Factions, Artifacts) that only repeat the lead of pages fetched here; other languages' pages; pages that merely mention the word Dovahkiin. They were judged from titles and search context, not opened.

known_limits: Dragon names that appear only inside English prose (e.g. the ships Kaal Kaaz, Sadon Reyth, Krilot Lok) are not collected unless a wiki sentence states a meaning or a speaker uses them in a quoted line.

Dialogue on pages that were not fetched is not covered. The page list was built from links, categories and word searches; a line that uses only dragon words no search term matched could have been missed.
Speaker names come from the wiki's labels, or else from the page subject or the narration before the quote; the basis is stated in each record's notes.
The wiki states no source for most word-wall translations; they are recorded as 'translation as given on the wiki page'.
The wiki's footnotes are not carried into the records. Each record names its page and revision, so the footnote behind a statement can be looked up there.

When the same dragon text stands on several pages, or several times on one page, one record is kept (other pages under also_on). A second English context or a differently worded gloss on another page is then not recorded, e.g. the gloss 'Ceaseless enemy!' for 'Unslaad hokoron!' on Skyrim:Alduin beside 'Unending enemy!' on Skyrim:Paarthurnax (dragon).
A dialogue record's english joins its segments' glosses line by line and writes '[no gloss on the wiki]' for a segment without one; use segments[] for aligned pairs.
Where the wiki sets one word outside a hover gloss (e.g. {{sic|Thurri|Thuri}} before the glossed rest of the sentence) the sentence is split into two segments as marked up.

verification_pass_2026-11-14.what: An independent check of this file against the raw wikitext (tools/ingest/verify_counts.py, a random sample, and a by-eye review of every word-list segment and every name record) led to these parser changes.
changes: Lore:Word Walls: where the inscription and transliteration columns differ (walls 'Diin' and 'Zul, Mey, Gut'), dovahzul is now the column that the shout page and the row's translation confirm (the inscription column); the other column is kept in transliteration_column.

Word-list matching: six hand-checked words or phrases (REVIEWED_TEXT in the parser) are taken as dragon text on their page, which repairs five cut-short or incomplete dialogue records; each such record says so in its notes.
Names: 'Dovah's Du'ul' no longer carries the English word 'Style' from the page title; Jun is glossed 'Light or Aether' as the sentence has it.
English context: the game's own placeholders in angle brackets (<man/woman>) are kept; only mark-up tags are removed.
Two more pages fetched and parsed: Lore:Vundeheim and Lore:Korvag Crag, each quoting a word wall already recorded from its shout page.

Dovahkiin, Dovahkiin, naal ok zin los vahriin, wah dein vokul mahfaeraak ahst vaal!
Ahrk fin norok paal graan fod nust hon zindro zaan, Dovahkiin, fah hin kogaan mu draal!

Wo lost fron wah ney dov, ahrk fin reyliik do jul, voth aan suleyk wah ronit faal krein!
Ahrk fin zul, rok drey kod, nau tol morokei frod, rul lot Taazokaan motaad voth kein!
Sahrot Thu'um, med aan tuz, vey zeim hokoron pah, ol fin Dovahkiin komeyt ok rein!
Ahrk fin Kel lost prodah, do ved viing ko fin krah, tol fod zeymah win kein meyz fundein!
Alduin, feyn do jun, kruziik vokun staadnau, voth aan bahlok wah diivon fin lein!
Nuz aan sul, fent alok, fod fin vul dovah nok, fen kos nahlot mahfaeraak ahrk ruz!
Paaz Keizaal fen kos stin nol bein Alduin jot, Dovahkiin kos fin saviik do muz!

texts.context: Hahaha! You have much to learn of the dov, then. There is nothing else but philosophy to a dovah. It is no accident that we do battle with our Thu'um, our Voices. There is no distinction between debate and combat to a dragon. Tinvaak los grah. For us it is one and the same.

texts.notes: Speaker from: page subject. english = the wiki editors' gloss (hover text or running text), not in-game text.
texts.context: If you can see your destiny clearly, your sight is clearer than mine. Dahmaan - remember, Alduin also follows his destiny, as he sees it. But, I bow before your certainty. In a way, I envy you. The curse of much knowledge is often indecision.

texts.location_or_speaker: Saying attributed to Dragons, recorded by Magnius Calussa in the book Wisdom of the Flying Gods (ESO: Elsweyr)
texts.notes: english is the in-book interpretation, which the author himself calls imperfect ('my interpretation of what those Words mean, imperfect though that interpretation may be'). Author's commentary: I first misunderstood this, for I thought that "lok" meant just "sky," and that we should look to the sky, but now I understand fully. It is not a command to look to the sky and seek help from above. It is a metaphor for flight. "Rise." Brace yourself and push yourself harder above the turbulent winds. Do not seek the safety of the ground. Rise and seek greater glory instead.

texts.notes: english is the in-book interpretation, which the author himself calls imperfect ('my interpretation of what those Words mean, imperfect though that interpretation may be'). Author's commentary: Be aware of your circumstances. Do not be so blind to your surroundings or focused on your goals that you forget to see the obvious dangers around you.

texts.location_or_speaker: Saying attributed to Dragons, recorded by Magnius Calussa in the book Wisdom of the Flying Gods (ESO: Elsweyr)
texts.dovahzul: Dey on folook fey ko ven ahrk ron.
texts.english: Implausible spirits haunt a grove in the wind and rain.
texts.notes: english is the in-book interpretation, which the author himself calls imperfect ('my interpretation of what those Words mean, imperfect though that interpretation may be'). Author's commentary: Whatever you think you see, look again. Look closer. Is there a more reasonable explanation? A note: The word "dey" seems to have a rather bawdy direct translation. At its core, it means "false," but has the connotation of "laughably false," laughing at those who make a claim. "On" is a little more slippery. I think it means something like "soul," but more empty. Something lifeless.
texts.translation_source: in-source (the book gives it)

texts.notes: No translation on the wiki, which says it cannot be translated completely. Wiki note: There are banners hanging throughout the High Hrothgar interior with two separate phrases written on them; either "LOK BO" or "THUUM TUUM". Unfortunately, it is impossible to translate them completely as not enough of the Dragon Language is known. We DO, however, know that "Lok" means "Sky" and "Thuum" means "Shout" or "Voice". Therefore, the most likely translation is a phrase that Arngeir commonly says when you engage or exit conversation with him: "Sky above, voice within."
